lines.text: Try snapping spaghetti in two. You almost never can.
Bend a dry stick from both ends, and it breaks into three pieces or more, nearly every time.
You'd guess it snaps at a weak spot, and the extra bits are just bad luck.
So slow it way down. The first crack opens near the middle, exactly as expected.
But the instant it breaks, each half springs back, and a wave of extra bending races along it.
Behind that wave, the stick bends even harder than when it first broke. So it cracks again.
Richard Feynman reportedly spent a whole evening trying to get just two pieces. He never managed it.
The snap-back explanation came in two thousand five, and it won an Ig Nobel Prize.
Then in two thousand eighteen, a team at MIT found the trick. Twist it first.
Turn the stick almost a full turn, then bend it slowly.
Now it breaks cleanly in two.
Twisted, it snaps with much less bend stored inside. The twist unwinds in a flash, and the leftover wave is too weak to crack it again.
Their model says about three quarters of a turn is enough. In the lab it took nearly a full one.
So twist, then bend slowly. The first break doesn't have to cause the second.
